title: Night buses and who the city runs for

turns.speaker: Dara
turns.text: They're cutting the last two night routes. The consultation says low ridership after one in the morning.

turns.speaker: Kofi
turns.text: Low compared to rush hour, which is not the comparison that matters for a service like that.

turns.speaker: Ines
turns.text: Everything after midnight will look bad against a Tuesday commute. You'd cut every rural route on that logic too.

turns.speaker: Dara
turns.text: Who actually uses them? Because the assumption in the room is drinkers.

turns.speaker: Kofi
turns.text: Cleaners, mostly. Hospital shifts, hotel staff, security, bakers. The people whose work makes the morning possible.

turns.speaker: Ines
turns.text: And overwhelmingly people who can't afford a taxi, which is the alternative being implicitly offered.

turns.speaker: Ines
turns.text: Cutting the bus isn't removing a journey. It's moving its cost onto the lowest-paid shift workers in the city.

turns.speaker: Dara
turns.text: There's a safety dimension too. Walking home at three is not the same risk for everyone.

turns.speaker: Kofi
turns.text: Which doesn't appear in a transport appraisal anywhere.

turns.speaker: Dara
turns.text: What would you actually do? The buses genuinely do run near empty some nights.

turns.speaker: Kofi
turns.text: Smaller vehicles, fewer routes, but keep something. A reduced service is a different thing from none.

turns.speaker: Ines
turns.text: And on-demand minibuses have worked in a few places, at a cost somewhere between a bus and a taxi.

turns.speaker: Dara
turns.text: That's at least an answer rather than a saving pretending to be one.

points: Night bus routes face closure on grounds of low ridership after 1am.
Kofi and Ines argue comparison with rush hour is inappropriate and would justify cutting rural services too.
Users are predominantly shift workers such as cleaners, hospital and hotel staff, rather than drinkers.
Ines argues cutting the service transfers costs to the lowest-paid workers, since taxis are the implicit alternative.
Walking home at night carries unequal safety risks that transport appraisals do not capture.
They propose smaller vehicles, reduced routes or on-demand minibuses rather than complete withdrawal.
